meta.title: Hausa A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hausa → English (see the Hausa, recall the meaning) and English → Hausa (see an English meaning, recall the Hausa). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms their background, their immediate surroundings and matters of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hausa, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 518 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and jobs, school, the months and the seasons, travel, the home and the kitchen, food and cooking, clothes, nature and animals, the body and health, feelings, free time, religion and festivals, the neighbourhood, and the everyday verbs, describing words and adverbs a simple account of one's day needs — and the other 232 are the commonest remaining words in the Tatoeba collection of Hausa sentences, counted by the WHOLE word (a noun's plural and its forms with the linker and the possessive endings added together). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hausa is ordinarily written, in the Latin alphabet with its hooked letters (ɓ ɗ ƙ and 'y); beneath it, where English Wiktionary gives one, is the same word with its TONES and VOWEL LENGTH marked, which ordinary writing leaves out: a high tone is unmarked, a low tone takes a grave accent (à), a falling tone a circumflex (â), and a long vowel a macron (ā) — ruwā 'water', màcḕ 'woman'. 419 of the 750 words have that line. 330 of the 750 are glossed by Folio itself rather than taken from Wiktionary, which lacks some of the commonest words in the language (yi 'to do', tafi 'to go', da 'and, with'); those carry no tone line, since a tone that no source states is not printed. The nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, and their plural, which in Hausa is seldom predictable, wherever the source gives them. Real example sentences come with 688 of the 750 words, three apiece for 519 of them, with the word picked out in colour; the sentences are as Tatoeba's contributors wrote them, which is not always with the hooks. There is no read-aloud button: few devices carry a Hausa voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Hausa Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the hooked letters and the other sounds English spelling has no letter for. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, tone, gender and plurals: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0), and Folio's own glosses for the words it lacks. Frequency and example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
